How I Built a Real-Time AI Program Intelligence Dashboard Using Jira MCP, Claude, and a Spreadsheet

A step-by-step guide to replacing manual status reports with a three-persona AI dashboard that shows leadership, GTM, and engineering exactly what they need — and nothing they don't.

Nehal Dixit
Senior TPM · PMP · SAFe RTE · AI-Augmented Delivery  ·  14 min read

Every Friday afternoon for years, I sat down to write status reports. Four engineering teams. Sixteen stakeholders. Three different audiences who all wanted the same data formatted completely differently. It took four hours every week and the information was stale by Monday morning.

Then I built something that changed how I work forever.

Using Jira's REST API, Claude's API, and a spreadsheet as the configuration layer, I built an AI-powered program intelligence dashboard that generates real-time delivery insights automatically. Three views. Three personas. Zero manual reporting. And the numbers speak for themselves: 32% improvement in delivery predictability and 22% throughput increase across four concurrent engineering squads.

This is the complete guide to how I built it — and how you can replicate it for your own programs.

"The goal was never to build a prettier dashboard. It was to eliminate the gap between when something goes wrong and when a stakeholder finds out about it."

The Problem With Traditional Program Reporting

Manual status reporting has three fundamental flaws that compound over time.

It's always stale. By the time you've pulled the Jira data, formatted it, written the narrative, and distributed it — the sprint has moved. Engineers have resolved blockers. New dependencies have emerged. The executive reading your Friday report is making decisions based on Tuesday's reality.

It's one-size-fits-all. Your CTO doesn't need sprint-level burndown details. Your QA lead doesn't need the executive release summary. But because reports are expensive to produce, you end up with one version that sort of works for everyone and actually works for nobody.

It's a TPM tax. Every hour spent compiling status is an hour not spent managing dependencies, unblocking engineers, or running the pre-PI syncs that actually prevent delivery failures.

What I wanted was a system where the data always reflected what was actually happening, each audience got exactly the view they needed, and the AI did the interpretation work so I didn't have to.

The Architecture — Three Components, One System

The system has three layers that work together.

The Spreadsheet — Your Configuration Layer. A structured Excel or Google Sheet that holds your program metadata — squad names, capacity per sprint, target versions, release dates, KPI definitions, and persona configurations. This is the "brain" that tells the system what your program looks like and who needs to see what.

Jira MCP — Your Live Data Layer. Using a Target Version JQL filter, the system pulls all issues that are part of the current release — and only those issues. Sprint velocity history, story point progress, dependency links, issue types, priorities, and SDLC stage all flow from Jira in real time. No manual extraction. No CSV exports.

Claude — Your Intelligence Layer. Claude receives the structured data from Jira combined with the configuration from your spreadsheet and generates three outputs: an executive summary for leadership, a release readiness digest for GTM, and a technical health analysis for engineering. Each output is calibrated for its audience — different language, different depth, different action orientation.

Step 1

Structure Your Spreadsheet

Before you write a single line of code or craft a single JQL query, your spreadsheet needs to be properly structured. This is the configuration layer that makes everything else work.

Tab 1: Program Config

This tab holds the global settings for your release program:

FieldExample ValuePurpose
Program NameEnterprise 9.0 ReleaseAppears in all dashboard headers
Target VersionLB-9.0-EnterpriseThe JQL filter key — only issues with this version are pulled
Release Date2026-03-31Used for all date forecasting calculations
Sprint Length14 daysDetermines sprint boundaries in velocity calculations
Buffer Percentage20%The pessimistic scenario buffer applied to story point projections
Scope Creep BaselineLast week issue countReference point for weekly scope change calculation

Tab 2: Squad Capacity

One row per squad, one column per sprint. This is where you capture both planned and actual capacity — accounting for holidays, PTO, and on-call rotations that your Jira data doesn't know about.

SquadSprint 114Sprint 115Sprint 116Sprint 117
Core80 pts75 pts80 pts65 pts (PTO)
Interop60 pts60 pts55 pts60 pts
SaaS70 pts70 pts70 pts70 pts
Cloud50 pts50 pts50 pts0 pts (blocked)

Why capacity lives in the spreadsheet and not Jira: Jira knows about story points. It doesn't know that two engineers are out next sprint, or that the Cloud team is blocked on an infrastructure dependency that has nothing to do with their Jira board. Your spreadsheet is the home for human context that no API can provide.

Tab 3: KPI Definitions

Define what success looks like for your program before the release starts — not after. This table becomes the scorecard Claude uses to generate its executive summary.

Step 2

Build Your Jira JQL Foundation

The single most important architectural decision in this entire system is using Target Version as your primary filter. This is what separates a release intelligence system from a generic Jira dashboard.

The Master Release JQL

Every query in the system starts with this filter. Nothing pulls data unless the issue belongs to the current release version:

fixVersion = "LB-9.0-Enterprise"
AND issuetype in (Story, Bug, Task, Sub-task)
ORDER BY priority DESC

This means when a new issue gets added to the release mid-sprint, it automatically appears in your dashboard. When an issue gets descoped, it disappears. The dashboard always reflects the real release scope — not a stale CSV export from three weeks ago.

Scope Creep Detection JQL

-- This week's count
fixVersion = "LB-9.0-Enterprise" AND created <= now()

-- Last week's count (for comparison)
fixVersion = "LB-9.0-Enterprise" AND created <= -7d

The delta between these two numbers — expressed as a percentage of last week's total — is your scope creep metric. Any increase above your configured warning threshold triggers a flag in the executive summary.

Dependency and Blocker Query

-- All blocked issues in the release
fixVersion = "LB-9.0-Enterprise"
AND issueType != Sub-task
AND issue in linkedIssues("is blocked by")
ORDER BY priority DESC

Common mistake: Many teams build dashboards using sprint filters instead of version filters. Sprint filters miss issues added to the release but not yet pulled into an active sprint — and include issues from previous sprints that are no longer relevant. Version filter gives you the cleanest release scope every time.

Step 3

Connect Jira MCP to Claude

This is where the system goes from a data pipeline to an intelligence system. Claude doesn't just display your Jira data — it interprets it, identifies risks, and generates human-readable summaries calibrated for each persona.

The MCP Connection Architecture

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the emerging standard for connecting AI agents to external tools and data sources. Think of it as USB-C for AI — any MCP-compatible agent can plug into any MCP-enabled data source without custom integration work.

Jira REST API → JQL queries → JSON response
           ↓
Spreadsheet config → capacity, KPIs, personas
           ↓
Combined context → Claude API prompt
           ↓
Three persona outputs → Dashboard views

The Data Assembly Function

async function assembleProgramContext(jiraConfig, sheetConfig) {
  const headers = {
    'Authorization': 'Basic ' + btoa(
      jiraConfig.email + ':' + jiraConfig.token
    ),
    'Accept': 'application/json'
  };

  const baseJQL = `fixVersion = "${jiraConfig.targetVersion}"`;

  const allIssues = await fetchJira(
    `/rest/api/3/search?jql=${baseJQL}&maxResults=500`, headers
  );
  const lastWeekIssues = await fetchJira(
    `/rest/api/3/search?jql=${baseJQL} AND created <= -7d`, headers
  );
  const blockers = await fetchJira(
    `/rest/api/3/search?jql=${baseJQL} AND issue in linkedIssues("is blocked by")`, headers
  );

  const totalIssues = allIssues.total;
  const doneIssues = allIssues.issues.filter(
    i => i.fields.status.statusCategory.key === 'done'
  ).length;
  const totalPoints = allIssues.issues.reduce(
    (sum, i) => sum + (i.fields.story_points || 0), 0
  );
  const donePoints = allIssues.issues
    .filter(i => i.fields.status.statusCategory.key === 'done')
    .reduce((sum, i) => sum + (i.fields.story_points || 0), 0);

  return {
    program: sheetConfig.programName,
    releaseDate: sheetConfig.releaseDate,
    totalIssues, doneIssues,
    issueCompletionPct: (doneIssues / totalIssues * 100).toFixed(1),
    totalPoints, donePoints,
    pointsCompletionPct: (donePoints / totalPoints * 100).toFixed(1),
    remainingPoints: totalPoints - donePoints,
    scopeCreepPct: ((totalIssues - lastWeekIssues.total) / lastWeekIssues.total * 100).toFixed(1),
    blockerCount: blockers.total,
    squadCapacity: sheetConfig.squadCapacity,
    kpiThresholds: sheetConfig.kpiDefinitions,
    velocityHistory: sheetConfig.velocityHistory
  };
}

The Three Persona Prompts

The quality of Claude's output depends entirely on how precisely you define the audience and what you want from them. Here are the prompts for each view:

Prompt 1: Leadership Executive Summary

You are an AI program intelligence system generating a weekly
executive summary for a CTO and VP audience.

Generate a 4-sentence executive summary that:
1. Opens with overall release health and one headline metric
2. Names the top risk with business impact quantified
3. States the release confidence level (High/Medium/Low) with reasoning
4. Ends with the single most important action required from leadership

Rules:
- No jargon. No bullet points. Write in complete sentences.
- Every risk must be expressed in business terms, not technical terms
- 4 sentences maximum. Stop after the 4th sentence.

Prompt 2: GTM Release Readiness

You are an AI program intelligence system generating a release
readiness brief for GTM, marketing, and product operations teams.

Generate a release readiness summary that:
1. States what is launch-ready versus still in progress
2. Flags any features that should be removed from launch communications
3. Lists 3 specific actions GTM teams need to take before release
4. Gives a launch confidence score: Go / Conditional Go / No-Go

Rules:
- Write for a non-technical audience
- Be specific about which features are ready and which are not
- Flag documentation gaps explicitly
- Keep total length under 150 words

Step 4

Build the Three Forecast Scenarios

The forecast engine is what transforms this from a status report into a decision-making tool. Using historical velocity data from Jira and capacity data from your spreadsheet, the system generates three scenarios for every release.

📉
Pessimistic

Historical velocity minus 20% buffer. Assumes new issues will be added, integration bugs will emerge, and at least one sprint will be disrupted. Shows the realistic worst-case completion date.

📈
Optimistic

Historical velocity maintained at current pace. No new scope added, no capacity disruptions. Shows what the completion date looks like if everything goes to plan.

📊
Realistic

Weighted hybrid of optimistic and pessimistic. Uses the last three sprints' velocity variance to calculate a confidence-weighted projection. This is the number I present to stakeholders.

function calculateForecasts(programContext) {
  const { remainingPoints, velocityHistory } = programContext;

  const recentVelocity = velocityHistory
    .slice(-3).reduce((sum, v) => sum + v, 0) / 3;

  const pessimistic = {
    velocityUsed: recentVelocity * 0.80,
    sprintsRemaining: Math.ceil(
      (remainingPoints * 1.20) / (recentVelocity * 0.80)
    ),
    label: 'Pessimistic (20% buffer + scope risk)'
  };

  const optimistic = {
    velocityUsed: recentVelocity,
    sprintsRemaining: Math.ceil(remainingPoints / recentVelocity),
    label: 'Optimistic (current pace maintained)'
  };

  const variance = calculateVelocityVariance(velocityHistory);
  const realisticVelocity = recentVelocity * (1 - variance * 0.5);

  const realistic = {
    velocityUsed: realisticVelocity,
    sprintsRemaining: Math.ceil(
      (remainingPoints * 1.10) / realisticVelocity
    ),
    label: 'Realistic (variance-weighted hybrid)'
  };

  return { pessimistic, optimistic, realistic };
}

The Real Goal: Transparency Across Business Units

The metrics are meaningful. But the real impact of this system is something harder to quantify: it eliminated the information asymmetry that causes most delivery failures.

Before this system, engineering knew what was blocked. Leadership didn't. GTM knew which features they were building launch materials around. Engineering didn't know which of those features were actually at risk. Everyone was working from a different snapshot of reality and nobody had the same picture.

The three-persona dashboard gives every stakeholder a view calibrated to their decision-making needs — but built from the same underlying data. When engineering sees a blocker flagged in the engineering view, leadership sees that same blocker expressed as a business risk in the executive view. The story is consistent. The language is different. Nobody is surprised.

"The goal of program management isn't to track what happened. It's to surface what's about to happen before it costs you."

Scope creep becomes visible the moment a new issue is added to the release version — not three weeks later when someone notices the burndown isn't burning. Velocity degradation surfaces in the trend line before it cascades into a missed milestone. Blockers that have been sitting unresolved for 96 hours get flagged in the AI summary before they become escalations.

That's the system working. Not faster reporting. Better decisions, earlier.

Getting Started in One Afternoon

If you want to replicate this system for your own program, here is the fastest path to a working prototype:

  1. Create your spreadsheet. Start with just two tabs: Program Config (target version, release date, buffer %) and Squad Capacity (squad names and sprint point targets). You can add KPIs and persona configuration later.
  2. Write your master JQL. Identify the Target Version in Jira that corresponds to your release and test the filter. Make sure it returns exactly the issues you expect — no more, no less.
  3. Get a Jira API token at id.atlassian.com/manage-profile/security/api-tokens and test your first API call using the JQL you just wrote.
  4. Get an Anthropic API key at console.anthropic.com and test a simple prompt with the program metrics from your first Jira call. Even a simple "summarize this sprint data for a VP audience" produces useful output immediately.
  5. Build the leadership view first. Get one AI-generated executive summary working end-to-end before you build the other two views. Prove the pipeline works before you scale it.
  6. Add the engineering and GTM views once the leadership view is stable. These require more data but the underlying architecture is identical.

You don't need Power BI. The system I built runs entirely in a browser as a single HTML file. The visualizations are built with standard web technologies. If you have a browser and two API keys, you can build this today.

The Bigger Picture

TPMs spend a significant percentage of their time on information logistics — gathering data, formatting it, translating it for different audiences, and distributing it to stakeholders who will act on it too slowly because it's already stale.

This system doesn't replace a TPM. It eliminates the part of the job that was never the real job. The dependency resolution, the stakeholder alignment, the hard conversations, the judgment calls under ambiguity — those still require a human being who understands the context. But the information logistics? That's exactly what AI was made for.

The future of technical program management isn't more sophisticated tracking. It's TPMs who build intelligent systems that give every stakeholder exactly the right information at exactly the right time — and then spend their own time on the work that actually moves programs forward.

Build the system. Then go do the work the system can't do for you.
